summary.text: After dividing the inclusion–exclusion formula by \((n-1)!\), the fixed-\(k\) term tends to \((-2)^k/k!\) (only the leading inner-sum contribution survives), and a summable factorial bound allows passage through the sum, giving \(e^{-2}\). The correction series tends to zero by the same dominated-convergence principle, while \(n!/(n-2)\sim(n-1)!\), so both sides are asymptotic to \(e^{-2}(n-1)!\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
(x)_k=x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1),\qquad (x)_0=1,
\]
denote the falling factorial. For natural-number arguments we use the usual convention that a binomial coefficient is zero if its lower argument exceeds its upper argument.

We begin with the exact inclusion–exclusion formula for the sequence. The finitely many values with \(n\leq 5\) do not affect an asymptotic assertion, so throughout the main argument we may assume \(n>5\). Put
\[
 S_{n,k}=\sum_{j=\max(0,k+5-n)}^{\min(k,4)}
 \binom{8-j}{j}\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}.
\]
Every summand in \(S_{n,k}\) is nonnegative. The given formula for A258667 is
\[
 a(n)=\left|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(n-1-k)!\,S_{n,k}\right|.
 \tag{1}
\]
(The absolute value is harmless in the original integer formula and makes explicit that \(a(n)\) is nonnegative.)

The correction sum in the conjectured expression is interpreted, for each fixed \(n\), over the indices for which its falling-factorial denominator is nonzero. Thus set
\[
 q_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Equivalently, one may extend this to a sum over all \(k\geq0\) by declaring the \(k=0\) term and every term whose denominator vanishes to be zero. The conjectured comparison function is therefore
\[
 b(n)=e^{-2}\frac{n!}{n-2}(1+q_n)
 \tag{3}
\]
for \(n>2\); its values at \(n\leq2\) may be defined arbitrarily, for instance as zero.

We will prove that both \(a(n)\) and \(b(n)\) are asymptotic to the same simpler function
\[
 h(n)=e^{-2}(n-1)!.
 \tag{4}
\]
This will establish \(a(n)\sim b(n)\).

First we record the elementary binomial limits needed below. For fixed nonnegative integers \(t,m\),
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n-t}{m}}{n^m}\longrightarrow \frac{2^m}{m!}.
 \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, once \(n\) is sufficiently large,
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n-t}{m}}{n^m}
 =\frac1{m!}\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\frac{2n-t-i}{n}
 =\frac1{m!}\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}
 \left(2-\frac{t+i}{n}\right).
\]
This is a fixed finite product, and each factor tends to \(2\), proving (5). More generally, if \(m<p\), then
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n-t}{m}}{n^p}\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{6}
\]
To see this, write the expression as the product of
\(\binom{2n-t}{m}/n^m\), which has a finite limit by (5), and
\(n^{-(p-m)}\), which tends to zero.

Fix \(k\). For all sufficiently large \(n\), the lower endpoint in the definition of \(S_{n,k}\) is zero, so its possible \(j\)-values are the fixed finite set
\(0\leq j\leq\min(k,4)\). Also, for such \(n\),
\[
2n+j-k-10=2n-(k+10-j).
\]
When \(j=0\), (5), with \(t=k+10\) and \(m=k\), gives
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n-k-10}{k}}{n^k}
 \longrightarrow \frac{2^k}{k!}.
\]
When \(j>0\), the lower argument of the binomial coefficient is \(k-j<k\), so (6) gives
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}}{n^k}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Consequently all the terms with \(j>0\) disappear in the limit. Since
\(\binom80=1\), finite summation yields
\[
 \frac{S_{n,k}}{n^k}\longrightarrow\frac{2^k}{k!}.
 \tag{7}
\]

We also have, for every fixed \(k\),
\[
 \frac{(n-1)_k}{n^k}
 =\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{i+1}{n}\right)
 \longrightarrow1.
 \tag{8}
\]
Dividing (7) by (8) and multiplying by \((-1)^k\) shows that, for
\[
 F_{n,k}=(-1)^k\frac{S_{n,k}}{(n-1)_k},
 \tag{9}
\]
we have the pointwise limit
\[
 F_{n,k}\longrightarrow\frac{(-2)^k}{k!}
 \qquad(n\to\infty)
 \tag{10}
\]
for every fixed \(k\).

To pass from these pointwise limits to the sum over \(k\), we need a bound uniform in \(n\). We now establish it carefully. Suppose first that \(k<n\), and let \(j\) be one of the indices occurring in \(S_{n,k}\). Then \(j\leq k\), \(j\leq4\), and, writing \(m=k-j\),
\[
 \binom{2n+j-k-10}{m}
 =\frac{(2n+j-k-10)_m}{m!}.
\]
For \(0\leq i<m\), comparison of the individual factors gives
\[
 2n+j-k-10-i\leq 2(n-1-i).
\]
Indeed, \(i\leq k-j-1\), and substituting this upper bound makes the inequality immediate. If a natural-number subtraction on the left has already reached zero, the inequality is even clearer. Multiplying these nonnegative inequalities gives
\[
 (2n+j-k-10)_m\leq 2^m(n-1)_m.
 \tag{11}
\]
Furthermore, because \(m=k-j\leq k\leq n-1\),
\[
 (n-1)_m\leq(n-1)_k.
 \tag{12}
\]
One way to see (12) is to extend the product defining \((n-1)_m\) by the factors
\(n-1-m,n-2-m,\ldots,n-k\); all of those are positive integers and hence at least one. Combining (11) and (12), we obtain
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}
 \leq \frac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}.
 \tag{13}
\]

Define
\[
 B_k=\sum_{j=0}^{4}\binom{8-j}{j}
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!},&j\leq k,\\[4pt]
 0,&j>k.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{14}
\]
Using the nonnegativity of \(S_{n,k}\), inequality (13), and enlarging the actual set of \(j\)-indices to all \(0\leq j\leq4\), we get
\[
 |F_{n,k}|\leq B_k\qquad(k<n).
 \tag{15}
\]
If \(k\geq n\), then \((n-1)_k=0\). We extend \(F_{n,k}\) by zero in this case; this agrees with the finite sum that will be used below. Thus (15) holds for all \(n,k\).

The sequence \((B_k)\) is summable. In fact, for each fixed \(j\), the nonzero part of the corresponding summand in (14), after the change of variable \(r=k-j\), is a constant multiple of
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{2^r}{r!}=e^2.
\]
There are only five choices of \(j\), so
\(\sum_{k\geq0}B_k<\infty\).

We may therefore apply the dominated convergence theorem for series (also known in this setting as Tannery's theorem) to (10) and (15). If
\[
 T_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}F_{n,k},
\]
then only the terms \(k<n\) are nonzero, and
\[
 T_n\longrightarrow
 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-2)^k}{k!}=e^{-2}.
 \tag{16}
\]

We next connect \(T_n\) exactly with the integer formula (1). For \(0\leq k<n\),
\[
 (n-1)!=(n-1-k)!(n-1)_k.
\]
Multiplying (9) by \((n-1)!\) therefore gives
\[
 (n-1)!F_{n,k}=(-1)^k(n-1-k)!S_{n,k}.

after summing from \(k=0\) to \(n-1\),
\[
 (n-1)!T_n=
 \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(n-1-k)!S_{n,k}.
\]
Taking absolute values and using (1), we obtain the exact identity
\[
 a(n)=(n-1)!\,|T_n| \qquad(n>5).
 \tag{17}
\]
Since the limit in (16) is the positive number \(e^{-2}\), continuity of absolute value gives
\[
 |T_n|\longrightarrow e^{-2}.
\]
It follows from (17) that
\[
 \frac{a(n)}{e^{-2}(n-1)!}
 =\frac{|T_n|}{e^{-2}}\longrightarrow1.
 \tag{18}
\]
Thus
\[
 a(n)\sim e^{-2}(n-1)!.
 \tag{19}
\]

It remains to compare the conjectured expression (3) with the same function. We first show
\[
 q_n\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{20}
\]
For this purpose define, for every \(k\geq0\),
\[
 G_{n,k}=
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k},&1\leq k<n,\\[5pt]
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then \(q_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}G_{n,k}\). For each fixed \(k\geq1\), equation (8) shows that \((n-1)_k\) grows like \(n^k\), hence tends to infinity; therefore
\(G_{n,k}\to0\). The same conclusion is immediate for \(k=0\), because that term was defined to be zero.

Moreover, whenever \(G_{n,k}\neq0\), the positive integer \((n-1)_k\) is at least one. Hence
\[
 |G_{n,k}|\leq\frac1{k!}
\]
for all \(n,k\). The majorant is summable because
\(\sum_{k\geq0}1/k!=e\). Dominated convergence for series now gives
\[
 q_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}G_{n,k}
 \longrightarrow\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}0=0,
\]
which proves (20).

Finally, for \(n>2\), use \(n!=n(n-1)!\) to compute
\[
 \frac{b(n)}{e^{-2}(n-1)!}
 =\frac{n}{n-2}(1+q_n).
 \tag{21}
\]
As \(n\to\infty\), the first factor on the right tends to \(1\), and the second tends to \(1\) by (20). Therefore
\[
 b(n)\sim e^{-2}(n-1)!.
 \tag{22}
\]
Combining (18) and (22), and observing that the common comparison function is always positive, yields
\[
 \frac{a(n)}{b(n)}
 = rac{a(n)/h(n)}{b(n)/h(n)}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \boxed{
 a(n)\sim e^{-2}\frac{n!}{n-2}
 \left(1+\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}\right)
 }
\]
with the sum interpreted, for each \(n\), over the admissible indices \(1\leq k<n\), as above. This is the claimed asymptotic equivalence.
